readingInstruction: Read 2 Chronicles 1:1-4:22. Solomon asks for wisdom and begins to build the temple. Read the account of the building as a picture of heaven on earth, and watch for where the Chronicler says the temple was built.
settingTheScene: 2 Chronicles begins with Solomon’s reign. The Chronicler tells the story with an emphasis on the temple and on Solomon’s early faithfulness, leaving out his later failures. Solomon goes to Gibeon to sacrifice, and God appears to him in a dream. Then the building begins on Mount Moriah, the site David purchased.
observation: “And Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great” (1:1).
“Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people” (1:10).
“Wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. I will also give you riches, possessions, and honor” (1:12).
“Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God” (2:4).
“But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him?” (2:6).
“Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah” (3:1).
“And he overlaid the house with gold” (3:7).
“And he made the veil of blue and purple and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and he caused cherubim to be embroidered on it” (3:14).
interpretation:
Solomon’s request for wisdom shows a humble heart. God offers anything, and Solomon asks not for riches or long life but for wisdom to govern God’s people. God grants it and adds the riches he did not ask for. There is a lesson: seek first what matters, and the rest is added.

The Chronicler lingers over the temple. He ties it to the past: it is built on Mount Moriah, “where the LORD had appeared to David his father,” the same site where Abraham offered Isaac in Genesis 22. The significance is that this place, associated with sacrifice and provision, is where God’s presence will dwell.

Solomon’s message to Hiram of Tyre contains a profound statement: “Heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him.” The temple is not meant to hold God. It is a place for his name, where he promises to meet his people. Solomon knows the paradox: the infinite God condescends to dwell among humans.

The building is described in lavish detail. Gold overlays the walls. Two great cherubim stand in the Most Holy Place. Two bronze pillars stand at the entrance, named Jachin and Boaz. The bronze altar, the molten sea, the lampstands, and the tables are all made by skilled workmen. The craftsmanship and beauty were part of the worship. God is worthy of the best.

To the returned exiles, the description of the first temple meant something. They had built a smaller one, and the old men wept. But the Chronicler tells them about Solomon’s temple to say, “This is the pattern. This is who God is. His presence once dwelled here, and he will come again.”
connection: John 2:19-21 says Jesus spoke of the temple of his body. 1 Corinthians 3:16 says “you are God’s temple and God’s Spirit dwells in you.” Ephesians 2:21-22 says the church is a holy temple in the Lord. James 1:5 promises wisdom to those who ask. Colossians 2:3: in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom. Acts 7:48: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. Revelation 21:22: no temple, for the Lord is its temple.
application:
Pray Solomon’s prayer for wisdom for a specific decision you face.

Remember that you are now a temple of the Spirit. Think about how you care for your body and your thoughts.

Offer your best skills to God, whatever they are.
prayerPrompts: Ask God for wisdom to lead those he has given you.
Marvel that heaven cannot contain him and yet he hears you.
Ask him to teach you to honor him in your work.
